title: Monitoring, Alarms & Access Control
metaDescription: Integrating monitoring, alarm management, and access control into a single operating picture for nuclear and critical-infrastructure security forces.
heroDek: Three systems, three vendors, three screens, one operator trying to correlate all of it in real time. That's not monitoring. That's a workload problem. GSS designs it as one picture.
contextHeading: Separate systems create a correlation problem for the human in the loop
contextParagraphs: Monitoring, alarm management, and access control are frequently procured, installed, and operated as three separate systems, each with its own interface, its own alarm logic, and its own vendor relationship. An operator watching all three is doing the correlation work manually, deciding whether a door alarm, a badge read, and a camera event fifteen seconds apart are the same story or three unrelated ones.

GSS designs monitoring, alarm management, and access control as one integrated capability rather than three adjacent systems. Access events, alarm state, and video assessment are tied together so an operator sees a correlated picture instead of three independent feeds, and alarm logic is tuned so genuine events are distinguishable from nuisance activity at the point they're raised, not fifteen minutes later during shift review.

The design work covers both ends of the system, from the credentialing and access-control policy that determines who can go where to the monitoring architecture that determines what the operator actually sees when something happens.

faq.q: Does this require replacing our existing access control system?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Integration is scoped against what's already in place; the design goal is a unified operating picture, which can mean new integration middleware rather than a wholesale system replacement.

faq.q: How is nuisance-alarm rate actually reduced without missing real events?
faq.a: Alarm logic is tuned using correlation across sensors, access events, and video rather than any single feed in isolation, so a nuisance source has to clear more than one check before it reaches the operator.

faq.q: Who ends up defining access privilege levels, GSS or the client?
faq.a: The client organization owns the policy decisions; GSS designs the system architecture and workflow that enforces and audits whatever policy the client sets.
